versions.text:
For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

In August the Orsk Gazette ran a photograph of Vell holding an empty trap beside the new sand fence. The fence had gone up along the dune foot over the winter, its slats set close and sunk a hand deep. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir, and visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass.

Arkin spent his first two nights under the boardwalk lamps and tallied eleven beetles. It was Vell who thought of the fence. Her notebooks held sixteen years of sketched night tracks, and nearly all of them crossed the dune foot where the slats now stood. At dusk the two of them knelt by the fence and watched beetles climb its face, slide back, and climb again until the tide turned.

Arkin asked whether the beetles would find their old crossings once the fence was opened. Vell took down the photograph pinned above her desk, from her first summer: the dune foot at night, streaked with tracks all the way to the water. She looked at it a long time, then said she used to stand there in the dark just to hear them pass, and that the sound had been gone since the slats went up.

Vell asked the park to cut gaps in the fence, a hand wide and ten metres apart. This July the count came back to five hundred and ninety.

For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence that ran the whole length of the dune foot, its slats a hand's width apart. A March storm tore away the dune's seaward face and much of the old crest with it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir, and visitors began to stray from it onto the dune. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass.

For a week Arkin walked the dune at dawn counting bootprints, and found nearly all of them in the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap. On the walk back he saw that the middle traps sat in loose sand on the landward slope. Vell's notebooks held a sketch of the dune drawn the day the traps were first set, and laid beside the dune as it now stood, it showed the crest twelve metres further inland. The beetles had moved with it, burrowing where the traps were no longer.

Arkin brought the sketch to Vell's desk and asked whether they should tell the park. Vell said he would be the one to tell them, and slid the season report across the desk. She had crossed out her own name on its first page and written his above it.

Vell moved the traps up onto the new crest. This July the count was seven hundred and eighty; last year's figure, she now writes, measured the traps rather than the beetles.

They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the south end of the dune foot, beside the car park. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened along the dune, and the park ran its lamps all night, every night. Visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap.

Arkin went first to the notebooks, reading all sixteen in search of an earlier drop that had recovered by itself. He found the 2013 drop, which had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass, and on a page from 2011 a note in Vell's hand: a camper's lamp left on the beach, and beetles heaped around it like spilled rice. That night the two of them walked the boardwalk and found the sand under every lamp crawling with beetles.

Arkin came back to the station at two in the morning with beetles in his hair and down his collar, held out his counter, and asked whether this many still counted as a drop. Vell lifted a beetle off his sleeve, set it on the windowsill, and asked it whether it had paid for its room at the boardwalk hotel.

Vell asked the park to put shades on the boardwalk lamps, so that their glow falls only on the planks. This July the count was six hundred and forty.

They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the dune foot, its slats a hand's width apart. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, and for two days seawater ran down the broken sand, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir. Visitors soon left it, wearing paths across the north hollow, where the middle traps stand, on their way to the water.

Arkin spent his first week on his knees along the fence, digging at its base for beetles caught against the slats, and found three. Vell went to her notebooks instead. Year after year they put the thickest burrows on the spit in the north hollow, and when she walked it at dawn the new paths had pressed the sand flat over the very patches her notebooks marked.

Arkin mentioned that the park planned to double the boardwalk's length next spring, and asked what she wanted to tell them. Vell spread the spit's map on the table, drew a line around the hollow, then drew a second line well outside the first, and said the park should see the second line before a single new post went in.

At Vell's request the park roped off the north hollow in August. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had recovered only after the park replanted the dune grass; this July the count was already six hundred and ten.

For sixteen summers Dr. Hana Vell has counted the sand beetles of Orsk Spit, pale hunters the size of a thumbnail. They spend the day in burrows in the upper dune and cross the dune foot each night to catch sand fleas along the tide line. Every July Vell sets forty pitfall traps along the dune crest. Last July, her student Joel Arkin's first on the spit, the count fell from its usual eight hundred to two hundred and sixty.

Much had changed on the spit that year. Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the south end of the dune foot, beside the car park. A March storm cut into the dune's seaward face, though the crest and the traps came through it. In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir; the park had wanted them on all night, but the power bill ran to nine thousand dollars a year. Visitors wore paths across the north hollow, a kilometre past the last trap.

Arkin spent his first week digging test pits where the storm had cut the dune, and found the burrows whole and full. Vell went to her notebooks. The spit's one earlier drop, in 2013, had looked just like this one: a fall by two thirds in a single July, then a slow climb back over two summers while the park left the dune as it was. It had recovered by itself.

Arkin brought Vell a letter asking the park to take down the fence and switch off the lamps, the third such letter he had drafted that week, and asked her to sign it. Vell handed it back unsigned, with the 2013 pages clipped to the front, and told him to read them before he wrote a fourth.

Vell left the traps and the spit exactly as they were. This July, with the fence, the lamps and the visitors all still there, the count climbed back to seven hundred and forty.
